title: Modern Indian History
summary: From Vasco da Gama to 1947: British expansion and the Governor-Generals, the Revolt of 1857, reform movements, early Congress, the Gandhian movements, revolutionaries, and the newspapers and books of the freedom struggle. It is the most-asked history block in SSC CGL. Expect 1–2 questions per shift, mostly event–year, reform–Governor-General and founder–organisation pairs.

subtopics.title: Europeans in India & British Expansion
subtopics.concept: European companies came to India by sea to trade, starting in 1498. The English East India Company slowly changed from a trader into a ruler. Two battles, Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764), gave it Bengal. Exams ask who came when, what each battle decided, and which Governor-General did what.

tricks.title: Plassey then Buxar: "57 buys, 64 seals"
tricks.body: **1757 Plassey** gave the British a foothold (Clive beat Siraj). **1764 Buxar** sealed control (three rulers beaten). The **Diwani** followed in **1765**.

example.q: Which battle was fought against the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II?
steps: Three rulers fought together.
Only Buxar had three Indian rulers on one side.

tricks.title: Governor-General reforms in order
tricks.body: Cornwallis **Settles** (1793) → Wellesley **Subsidises** (1798) → Bentinck bans **Sati** (1829) → Ripon starts **Local** self-government (1882).

mistakes.wrong: Calling Warren Hastings the first Governor-General of India.
mistakes.right: Warren Hastings = first GG of **Bengal** (1773). Bentinck = first GG of **India** (1833). Canning = first **Viceroy** (1858).

mistakes.wrong: Placing the Ilbert Bill in Curzon's time.
mistakes.right: The Ilbert Bill (1883) belongs to **Ripon**.

mistakes.wrong: Saying the English set up their first factory at Calicut.
mistakes.right: The English factory was at **Surat**. Calicut is where **Vasco da Gama** landed.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking the Diwani (1765) made the Company owner of the land.
mistakes.right: Diwani was only the right to **collect revenue** in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

mistakes.wrong: Putting Awadh (1856) under the Doctrine of Lapse.
mistakes.right: Awadh was annexed for **misgovernment**. Lapse states include Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing Ryotwari and Mahalwari.
mistakes.right: **Ryot**wari = deal with each **ryot** (Madras, Bombay). **Mahal**wari = deal with the village **mahal** (North-West).

subtopics.notes:
### The Europeans arrive
Five European powers came to trade. Learn them in the order they arrived.

| Power | Year | Remember |
|---|---|---|
| **Portuguese** | **1498** | **Vasco da Gama** landed near **Calicut** (Kappad); the ruler was the Zamorin. **Albuquerque** took **Goa (1510)**. |
| **English** | **31 Dec 1600** | Charter from **Elizabeth I**. First permanent factory at **Surat (1613)**, after a naval win over the Portuguese. |
| Dutch | 1602 | VOC; Pulicat, Masulipatnam. Lost to the English at **Bedara (1759)**. |
| Danish | 1616 | Tranquebar, Serampore |
| **French** | **1664** | Company formed under **Colbert**; **Pondicherry (1674)**; **Dupleix** was the key governor |

The English then built three presidencies: **Madras (1639)**, **Bombay (1668**, part of Charles II's dowry) and **Calcutta (1690**, Job Charnock).

> **Tip:** Order of arrival: Portuguese, English, Dutch, Danish, French. Remember "**P**lease **E**at **D**al, **D**on't **F**ight".

### Plassey and Buxar: from trader to ruler
The Company first beat the French, then took Bengal.

| Battle | Date | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| **Plassey** | **23 June 1757** | **Robert Clive** defeated **Siraj-ud-Daulah**. **Mir Jafar** betrayed Siraj. |
| Wandiwash | 1760 | **Eyre Coote** defeated the French general Lally. This ended French hopes (Third Carnatic War). |
| **Buxar** | **22 Oct 1764** | **Hector Munro** defeated three rulers together: **Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Emperor Shah Alam II**. |

The **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)** gave the Company the **Diwani** of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Diwani means the right to collect revenue. It did not mean owning the land. Clive then ran a "dual government" (1765–72). **Warren Hastings** ended it.

### Wars that built the empire
| Wars | Years | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Anglo-Mysore (four wars) | 1767–1799 | Fought against Haidar Ali and **Tipu Sultan**, the "Tiger of Mysore". Tipu died defending **Srirangapatna in 1799** (Fourth war, Wellesley's time). |
| Anglo-Maratha (three wars) | 1775–1818 | First war ended by the **Treaty of Salbai (1782)**. The third war ended Peshwa rule (**1818**). |
| Anglo-Sikh (two wars) | 1845–49 | Fought after Ranjit Singh's death (1839). **Punjab annexed 1849** (Dalhousie). |

Other gains: Sind (1843, Napier), Burma, and **Awadh (1856)**, taken "for misgovernment".

### Two tools of annexation
- **Subsidiary Alliance** (**Wellesley**, **1798**): an Indian ruler kept Company troops at his cost. He lost his independence. The **Nizam of Hyderabad** signed first.
- **Doctrine of Lapse** (**Dalhousie**): if a ruler died without a son, an adopted heir was not accepted. The state "lapsed" to the Company. Examples: **Satara, Jaitpur, Sambalpur, Udaipur, Jhansi, Nagpur**.

> **Watch:** Awadh was annexed for "misgovernment", not under the Doctrine of Lapse.

### Governors-General and Viceroys
| Name | Remember for |
|---|---|
| **Warren Hastings** | First Governor-General of **Bengal** (Regulating Act 1773). Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784, founded by William Jones). Pitt's India Act 1784 added dual control. |
| **Cornwallis** (1786–93) | **Permanent Settlement (1793)**; police and judicial reforms; "father of the civil services" |
| **Wellesley** | **Subsidiary Alliance** (1798) |
| **William Bentinck** (1828–35) | First Governor-General of **India** (Charter Act 1833); **sati abolished (1829)**; English Education Act 1835 (Macaulay's Minute); thuggee suppressed |
| **Dalhousie** (1848–56) | Doctrine of Lapse; first railway **Bombay–Thane (16 April 1853)**; telegraph; postage; engineering colleges; Wood's Despatch (1854) |
| **Canning** | Last Governor-General and **first Viceroy (1858)** |
| **Lytton** | Delhi Durbar 1877 (Victoria made "Empress of India"); **Vernacular Press Act 1878**; Arms Act |
| **Ripon** | "Father of **local self-government**" (1882); **Ilbert Bill** (1883); first synchronous **census (1881)** |
| Dufferin | Congress founded (1885) |
| **Curzon** | **Partition of Bengal (1905)**; Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904) |
| Hardinge II | 1911: capital to shift to **Delhi**; partition annulled |
| Mountbatten | Last Viceroy; first Governor-General of free India |

**C. Rajagopalachari** was the last, and the only Indian, Governor-General.

### Three land-revenue systems
| System | Region | Who and how |
|---|---|---|
| **Permanent Settlement (1793)** | Bengal, Bihar, Odisha | **Cornwallis**. Zamindars became landowners. Revenue fixed forever. |
| **Ryotwari** | Madras, Bombay | Reed and **Thomas Munro**. Deal made directly with the **ryot** (the farmer). |
| **Mahalwari** | North-Western Provinces, Central India, parts of Punjab | **Holt Mackenzie, 1822**. Deal made with the **village estate (mahal)**. |

patterns.name: Plassey → Buxar → Diwani chain
patterns.howToSpot: The question names Plassey, Buxar, Mir Jafar, Shah Alam II or the Treaty of Allahabad.
steps: Plassey 1757 = Clive against Siraj-ud-Daulah; Mir Jafar betrayed.
Buxar 1764 = Hector Munro against Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II.
Treaty of Allahabad 1765 = Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa.
Match the name in the question to one of these three lines.
patterns.why: These three events form one chain, so each fact points to the next.

example.q:
The Battle of Buxar (1764) was fought against a combined army of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and:
(a) Siraj-ud-Daulah (b) Shah Alam II (c) Tipu Sultan (d) Mir Jafar
steps: Siraj-ud-Daulah fought at Plassey, so cut (a).
Mir Jafar was the traitor at Plassey, so cut (d).
Tipu fought the Mysore wars, so cut (c).

patterns.name: Anglo-Mysore, Anglo-Maratha and Anglo-Sikh wars
patterns.howToSpot: Words like "Tipu Sultan died in", "which war ended Maratha power", "Punjab was annexed in".
steps: Mysore: four wars; Tipu died at Srirangapatna, 1799.
Marathas: three wars; Treaty of Salbai (1782) ended the first; power ended 1818.
Sikhs: two wars; Punjab annexed 1849 under Dalhousie.
patterns.why: Each group of wars has one number and one end year; that is what the options test.

example.q: Tipu Sultan was killed in 1799 while defending:
steps: 1799 is the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.
Tipu died defending his capital.

patterns.name: Governor-General ↔ measure
patterns.howToSpot: "Sati was abolished by", "Vernacular Press Act was passed by", "first railway under" — a measure and a ruler.
steps: Recall the one-line table: Cornwallis, Wellesley, Bentinck, Dalhousie, Lytton, Ripon, Curzon.
Check the year given in the question against the ruler's time.
In "wrongly matched" questions, look for a measure swapped with a neighbour.
patterns.why: Each Governor-General is remembered for one or two measures, so the pair decides the answer.

example.q:
The Vernacular Press Act (1878) was passed during the time of:
(a) Ripon (b) Lytton (c) Curzon (d) Dalhousie
steps: 1878 falls between Dalhousie (1850s) and Ripon (1880s).
Ripon repealed the Act in 1882, so cut (a).
Lytton held the Delhi Durbar in 1877 and passed this Act in 1878.

patterns.name: Land-revenue systems
patterns.howToSpot: Words like zamindar, ryot, mahal, Permanent Settlement, Thomas Munro or Holt Mackenzie.
steps: Permanent Settlement 1793: Cornwallis, Bengal-Bihar-Odisha, zamindars.
Ryotwari: Reed and Thomas Munro, Madras and Bombay, each farmer.
Mahalwari: Holt Mackenzie 1822, North-West, village estate.
patterns.why: The name of each system tells you who pays: zamindar, ryot or mahal.

example.q: The Ryotwari system, which settled revenue directly with each farmer, was mainly used in:
steps: "Ryot" means the farmer.
Ryotwari is linked with Reed and Thomas Munro in the south and west.

patterns.name: European arrival: who came where and when
patterns.howToSpot: "Vasco da Gama landed at", "first English factory", "French headquarters", or a list of European powers.
steps: Recall the arrival table: Portuguese 1498, English 1600, Dutch 1602, Danish 1616, French 1664.
Attach one place to each: Calicut, Surat, Pulicat, Tranquebar, Pondicherry.
Pick the option that matches both the power and the place.
patterns.why: Each power has one landmark year and one landmark place.

example.q:
The English East India Company set up its first permanent factory at:
(a) Calicut (b) Surat (c) Pondicherry (d) Goa
steps: Calicut = Vasco da Gama (Portuguese), so cut (a).
Pondicherry = French; Goa = Portuguese under Albuquerque.

patterns.name: Arrange in chronological order
patterns.howToSpot: "Arrange the following in the correct order" with 3 or 4 battles, treaties or measures.
steps: Write the year next to each item.
Find the earliest item and check which options start with it.
Check the last item to split any options that remain.
patterns.why: Checking only the first and last items usually leaves one option, which saves time.

example.q: Arrange in order: 1. Treaty of Allahabad 2. Battle of Plassey 3. Battle of Wandiwash 4. Battle of Buxar
steps: Years: Allahabad 1765, Plassey 1757, Wandiwash 1760, Buxar 1764.
Earliest is Plassey (2); latest is Allahabad (1).

patterns.name: First and last titles
patterns.howToSpot: "First Governor-General of Bengal/India", "first Viceroy", "last Viceroy", "only Indian Governor-General".
steps: First GG of Bengal = Warren Hastings (1773).
First GG of India = William Bentinck (1833).
Last GG and first Viceroy = Canning (1858).
Last Viceroy = Mountbatten; last and only Indian GG = C. Rajagopalachari.
patterns.why: The title changed twice (1833 and 1858), so read the exact title in the question.

example.q: Who was the first Governor-General of India?
steps: "Of India" (not "of Bengal") starts with the Charter Act of 1833.
Warren Hastings was GG of Bengal, so he is the trap option.

revision: Arrival: Portuguese 1498, English 1600, Dutch 1602, Danish 1616, French 1664.
Plassey 1757 (Mir Jafar's betrayal) → Buxar 1764 (three rulers) → Diwani 1765 (Treaty of Allahabad).
Tipu died at Srirangapatna 1799; Peshwa rule ended 1818; Punjab annexed 1849.
Wellesley = Subsidiary Alliance; Dalhousie = Doctrine of Lapse + railways (1853).
Cornwallis = Permanent Settlement 1793; Bentinck = sati abolished 1829.
Lytton = Vernacular Press Act 1878; Ripon = local self-government 1882; Curzon = Bengal partition 1905.
Revenue: Permanent (Cornwallis), Ryotwari (Munro), Mahalwari (Holt Mackenzie).

subtopics.title: Revolt of 1857 and Peasant & Tribal Uprisings
subtopics.concept: In 1857, Indian soldiers of the Company army, called sepoys, rose in revolt. It spread across north and central India before the British crushed it. In 1858 the British Crown took over India from the Company. Peasant and tribal revolts are asked in the same set of questions.

tricks.title: 1857 pairs: "Kanpur Nana, Lucknow Lady, Jhansi Rani, Bihar Kunwar"
tricks.body: **K**anpur–**N**ana Saheb · **L**ucknow–Begum Hazrat Mahal (the Lady) · **J**hansi–Rani Lakshmibai · **B**ihar (Jagdishpur)–Kunwar Singh, the old hero.

example.q: Kunwar Singh led the revolt of 1857 in which region?
steps: "Bihar Kunwar" in the memory line.
His home was Jagdishpur; he fought at Arrah.

mistakes.wrong: Saying the revolt broke out at Barrackpore.
mistakes.right: Barrackpore was Mangal Pandey's earlier act (29 March). The revolt **broke out at Meerut** (10 May 1857).

mistakes.wrong: Saying Colin Campbell defeated Rani Lakshmibai.
mistakes.right: Rani Lakshmibai was defeated by **Hugh Rose**. Campbell fought at Kanpur and Lucknow.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Bahadur Shah Zafar was sent to the Andamans.
mistakes.right: He was exiled to **Rangoon**.

mistakes.wrong: Linking Kunwar Singh with Gwalior.
mistakes.right: Kunwar Singh fought in **Bihar** (Arrah, Jagdishpur). Gwalior is where the Rani died.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the greased cartridge the main cause.
mistakes.right: It was only the **immediate** cause. The deeper causes were political, economic, social and military.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing the Santhal Hul and the Munda Ulgulan.
mistakes.right: Santhal Hul 1855–56 = **Sidhu and Kanhu**. Munda Ulgulan 1899–1900 = **Birsa Munda**.

subtopics.notes:
### The spark: greased cartridges
The revolt had one quick trigger and many deeper causes. The trigger was a rumour about the new **Enfield rifle**.

Its cartridges were said to be greased with **cow and pig fat**. Soldiers had to bite them open. This was only the **immediate cause**.

| Date | Place | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| **29 March 1857** | **Barrackpore** | **Mangal Pandey** of the **34th Native Infantry** attacked his officers. He was hanged on 8 April. |
| **10 May 1857** | **Meerut** | 85 troopers of the 3rd Light Cavalry had been jailed for refusing the cartridges. The sepoys broke out and marched to Delhi. |
| Next | Delhi | They proclaimed the old **Bahadur Shah II (Zafar)** "Emperor of India". |

> **Watch:** Barrackpore was the first spark. The revolt itself **broke out at Meerut** on 10 May.

### Deeper causes
- **Political:** Doctrine of Lapse (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur); Awadh annexed (1856); disrespect to the Mughal family; Nana Saheb's pension stopped.
- **Economic:** heavy land revenue; ruin of handicrafts; drain of wealth; loss of zamindari and talukdari rights.
- **Social and religious:** reform laws such as sati abolition; the Religious Disabilities Act (1850) let converts inherit property; rumours about railways and telegraphs; missionary work.
- **Military:** poor pay and promotion; Indians kept out of officer ranks; the **General Service Enlistment Act (1856)** meant service across the sea, which many feared would cost them caste.

> **Tip:** In a "which was NOT a cause" question, look for an event after 1857, such as the Partition of Bengal.

### Centres, leaders and British officers
| Centre | Indian leader | British officer |
|---|---|---|
| Delhi | Bahadur Shah II; General **Bakht Khan** | John Nicholson, Hodson |
| **Kanpur** | **Nana Saheb**, with **Tantia Tope** and Azimullah Khan | Colin Campbell |
| **Lucknow** | **Begum Hazrat Mahal** | Colin Campbell |
| **Jhansi** | **Rani Lakshmibai** | **Hugh Rose** |
| **Arrah / Jagdishpur (Bihar)** | **Kunwar Singh**, aged about 80 | William Taylor, Vincent Eyre |
| Faizabad | **Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah** | — |
| **Bareilly** | **Khan Bahadur Khan** | — |

The revolt spread through the Ganga plain, central India and parts of the Deccan. Bombay, Madras, Bengal proper and most of Punjab stayed quiet. Some historians call it a "sepoy mutiny". **V.D. Savarkar** called it the "**First War of Independence**".

### How it ended
- **September 1857:** the British took back Delhi. Bahadur Shah was tried and exiled to **Rangoon**. Hodson shot his sons.
- **June 1858:** Rani Lakshmibai died fighting at **Gwalior**.
- **1859:** Tantia Tope was captured and hanged.

The **Governor-General** during the revolt was **Canning**.

### The Act of 1858
The **Government of India Act, 1858** ended Company rule. India came under the British **Crown**.
- A **Secretary of State for India** took charge in London.
- The Governor-General got the title **Viceroy**. **Canning** was the first.
- **Queen Victoria's Proclamation** was read at **Allahabad on 1 November 1858**. It promised no more annexations and no interference in religion.
- The army was rebuilt on "divide and rule" lines.

### Peasant and tribal uprisings
| Movement | Year | Region | Leader or key fact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Paika rebellion** | 1817 | Odisha | **Bakshi Jagabandhu**; against the British land system |
| Kol uprising | 1831 | Chotanagpur | Tribal lands taken by outsiders |
| **Santhal Hul** | 1855–56 | Rajmahal hills (Jharkhand) | **Sidhu and Kanhu** Murmu; against moneylenders and revenue men |
| **Indigo revolt** | 1859–60 | Bengal | The play *Neel Darpan* by Dinabandhu Mitra |
| **Munda Ulgulan** | 1899–1900 | Chotanagpur | **Birsa Munda** ("Dharti Aba"); led to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908) |
| Faraizi movement | — | Bengal | Dudu Mian |
| Moplah uprising | peak 1921 | Malabar (Kerala) | Linked to the Khilafat movement |
| **Bardoli Satyagraha** | 1928 | Gujarat | **Vallabhbhai Patel**; he earned the title **"Sardar"** |
| Tebhaga | 1946 | Bengal | Sharecroppers asked for two-thirds of the crop |

patterns.name: 1857 centre ↔ leader
patterns.howToSpot: "Who led the revolt at…", or a match-the-column of centres and leaders.
steps: Recall the seven pairs: Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Arrah, Faizabad, Bareilly.
Remember the helpers too: Tantia Tope (Kanpur), Bakht Khan (Delhi).
Match first the pairs you are surest of, then cut options.
patterns.why: Every centre had one main leader, so one sure pair removes most options.

example.q: Match: A. Kanpur B. Lucknow C. Jhansi D. Bareilly with 1. Begum Hazrat Mahal 2. Khan Bahadur Khan 3. Nana Saheb 4. Rani Lakshmibai
steps: Kanpur–Nana Saheb (3); Lucknow–Hazrat Mahal (1).
Jhansi–Lakshmibai (4); Bareilly–Khan Bahadur Khan (2).

patterns.name: Causes: immediate trigger and deeper causes
patterns.howToSpot: "Immediate cause of the revolt", "General Service Enlistment Act", or "which was NOT a cause".
steps: Immediate cause = greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle.
Deeper causes: political, economic, social-religious, military.
For a "NOT a cause" option, pick anything that happened after 1857.
patterns.why: A cause must come before the event, so later events are always wrong.

example.q:
Which of these was NOT a cause of the Revolt of 1857?
(a) Doctrine of Lapse (b) General Service Enlistment Act (c) Partition of Bengal (d) Annexation of Awadh
steps: Lapse, Awadh (1856) and the 1856 Act all came before 1857.
The Partition of Bengal came in 1905.

patterns.name: Course of the revolt and the Act of 1858
patterns.howToSpot: "The revolt began at Meerut on", Bahadur Shah's fate, or what the 1858 Act did.
steps: Timeline: Barrackpore 29 March → Meerut 10 May 1857 → Delhi → Delhi falls September 1857.
Bahadur Shah II: tried and exiled to Rangoon.
1858 Act: Crown rule, Secretary of State, Viceroy (Canning), Queen's Proclamation.
patterns.why: The 1858 Act is the one big change that followed the revolt.

example.q: The Government of India Act, 1858 did which of these?
steps: It ended Company rule; the Crown took over.
A Secretary of State was created; Canning became the first Viceroy.
example.answer: Transferred rule from the East India Company to the British Crown

patterns.name: Peasant or tribal uprising ↔ leader
patterns.howToSpot: "The Santhal rebellion was led by", Birsa Munda, Paika rebellion, Bardoli, Tebhaga.
steps: Recall the uprisings table: movement, year, region, leader.
Tie each tribe to its leader: Santhal–Sidhu and Kanhu, Munda–Birsa.
Use the region to cut options: Odisha, Chotanagpur, Bengal, Malabar, Gujarat.
patterns.why: Each uprising has one leader and one region, and the options mix them up.

example.q: The Santhal rebellion of 1855–56, called the Hul, was led by:
steps: Santhal = Sidhu, by the first letter.
Birsa Munda led the Munda Ulgulan, a different tribe.

patterns.name: British officer who crushed the revolt
patterns.howToSpot: "Who suppressed the revolt at…" or "Hugh Rose fought against".
steps: Jhansi → Hugh Rose.
Kanpur and Lucknow → Colin Campbell.
Delhi → John Nicholson, Hodson.
Bihar → William Taylor, Vincent Eyre.
patterns.why: Only four British names repeat, so the centre fixes the officer.

example.q:
The British officer who defeated Rani Lakshmibai was:
(a) Colin Campbell (b) Hugh Rose (c) John Nicholson (d) Hodson
steps: Campbell = Kanpur and Lucknow; Nicholson and Hodson = Delhi.
Jhansi = Hugh Rose.

patterns.name: Order of uprisings
patterns.howToSpot: "Arrange these movements in chronological order" with tribal or peasant revolts.
steps: Write the year next to each: Paika 1817, Kol 1831, Santhal 1855, Indigo 1859, Munda 1899.
Later ones: Moplah 1921, Bardoli 1928, Tebhaga 1946.
Check the first and last items against the options.
patterns.why: Years are far apart, so sorting takes seconds once the years are known.

example.q: Arrange in order: 1. Munda Ulgulan 2. Paika rebellion 3. Santhal Hul 4. Indigo revolt
steps: Paika 1817, Santhal 1855, Indigo 1859, Munda 1899.
So the order is 2, 3, 4, 1.

revision: Trigger: greased Enfield cartridges (cow and pig fat rumour).
Barrackpore, 29 March 1857 (Mangal Pandey) → Meerut, 10 May 1857 (outbreak) → Delhi.
Kanpur–Nana Saheb, Lucknow–Hazrat Mahal, Jhansi–Lakshmibai, Arrah–Kunwar Singh, Bareilly–Khan Bahadur Khan.
Hugh Rose defeated the Rani; Colin Campbell took Kanpur and Lucknow.
Bahadur Shah II exiled to Rangoon; Delhi fell in September 1857.
Act of 1858: Crown rule, Secretary of State, Canning first Viceroy; Proclamation at Allahabad, 1 Nov 1858.
Uprisings: Paika 1817, Kol 1831, Santhal 1855, Indigo 1859, Munda 1899, Bardoli 1928, Tebhaga 1946.

subtopics.title: Socio-Religious Reform Movements
subtopics.concept: In the 19th century, Indian reformers fought practices like sati, child marriage and caste discrimination. They set up groups called Samaj or Sabha. Exams ask the founder, the year and the main aim of each group, and the laws reformers pushed for.

tricks.title: 1875: the year of three
tricks.body: **Arya Samaj** (Dayanand), **Theosophical Society** (Blavatsky and Olcott) and the **Aligarh MAO College** (Sir Syed) all date to **1875**.

example.q: Which two of these began in the same year: Arya Samaj, Brahmo Samaj, Theosophical Society, Ramakrishna Mission?
steps: Brahmo 1828, Ramakrishna Mission 1897.
Arya Samaj 1875 and Theosophical Society 1875.

tricks.title: Founder hooks by first letter
tricks.body: **R**am Mohan = **R**eform of sati (Brahmo, 1828) · **D**ayanand = **D**iscover the Vedas (Arya) · **P**hule = **P**eople of lower castes (Satyashodhak) · **V**ivekananda = **V**edanta and service (Ramakrishna Mission, 1897).

mistakes.wrong: Saying Ramakrishna Paramahamsa founded the Ramakrishna Mission.
mistakes.right: It was founded by his disciple **Vivekananda** in **1897**.

mistakes.wrong: Saying the Theosophical Society was founded at Adyar.
mistakes.right: It was founded in **New York** (1875). Its Indian headquarters moved to Adyar later.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the 1856 Widow Remarriage Act to Ram Mohan Roy.
mistakes.right: 1856 widow remarriage = **Vidyasagar**. 1829 sati abolition = Ram Mohan Roy's campaign.

mistakes.wrong: Swapping Prarthana Samaj and Brahmo Samaj.
mistakes.right: Prarthana = 1867, Bombay, Atmaram Pandurang. Brahmo = 1828, Calcutta, Ram Mohan Roy.

mistakes.wrong: Placing the Self-Respect Movement in Kerala.
mistakes.right: Self-Respect (1925) = **Periyar**, Tamil Nadu. Kerala = Sree Narayana Guru, SNDP Yogam (1903).

subtopics.notes:
### Ram Mohan Roy and the Brahmo Samaj
**Raja Ram Mohan Roy** is called the "father of modern India". He began the reform age in Bengal.

- **Atmiya Sabha (1815)**: the group that came before the Brahmo Samaj.
- **Brahmo Sabha / Samaj (1828)**: belief in one God (monotheism) and no idol worship.
- He campaigned against **sati**. It was abolished in **1829** under Bentinck.
- He also worked for widow remarriage, a free press and English education. He wrote *Gift to Monotheists*.

Later the Brahmo Samaj was led, through its splits, by **Debendranath Tagore** (Tattvabodhini Sabha, 1839) and **Keshab Chandra Sen**.

**Young Bengal (1820s)**: radical students of Hindu College led by **Henry Vivian Derozio**.

### Organisations to know
| Organisation | Year | Founder | Remember for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prarthana Samaj** | 1867 | **Atmaram Pandurang** (Bombay) | **M.G. Ranade**, R.G. Bhandarkar; worship of God plus social reform |
| **Satyashodhak Samaj** | **1873** | **Jyotirao Phule** | Book ***Gulamgiri*** (1873); rights of lower castes |
| Singh Sabha | 1873 | Amritsar | Sikh revival |
| **Arya Samaj** | **1875** | **Swami Dayanand Saraswati** (Bombay) | ***Satyarth Prakash***; "Back to the Vedas"; **shuddhi** (reconversion); DAV schools |
| **Theosophical Society** | 1875 | **Madame Blavatsky and Col. Olcott** (New York) | Indian headquarters at **Adyar, Madras (1882)**; **Annie Besant** led it later |
| Aligarh Movement | 1875 | **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** | Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental (MAO) College → **AMU (1920)**; modern education for Muslims |
| Deccan Education Society | 1884 | Tilak and Agarkar | Fergusson College |
| **Ramakrishna Mission** | **1897** | **Swami Vivekananda** | Belur Math; service to people; Chicago speech 1893 |
| Servants of India Society | 1905 | **Gokhale** | Trained public workers |

> **Tip:** **1875** is the year of three: Arya Samaj, Theosophical Society and the Aligarh MAO College.

> **Watch:** The Ramakrishna Mission was founded by **Vivekananda**, not by Ramakrishna Paramahamsa himself.

### Vidyasagar and the reform laws
**Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** turned the widow-remarriage campaign into law. He sent petitions, argued from Sanskrit texts and raised a fund for remarried widows. He also wrote the Bengali primer *Borno Porichoy*.

| Year | Law | Reformer behind it |
|---|---|---|
| **1829** | Bengal Sati Regulation (Regulation XVII) | Ram Mohan Roy (signed by Bentinck) |
| **1856** | **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act** | **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** |
| **1891** | Age of Consent Act (age raised to 12) | Behramji Malabari |
| **1929** | **Sarda Act** (Child Marriage Restraint Act) | Har Bilas Sarda; marriage age **18 for boys, 14 for girls** |

> **Rule:** The law years go 1829, 1856, 1891, 1929. Each is roughly a generation apart.

### Lower-caste and regional movements
- **Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule**: Satyashodhak Samaj (1873); Pune's first girls' school (1848).
- **Sree Narayana Guru** (Kerala, Ezhava community): set up the Aruvippuram Shiva shrine (1888). He inspired the **SNDP Yogam (1903)**. Motto: "One caste, one religion, one God for man".
- **Periyar E.V. Ramasamy**: **Self-Respect Movement (1925)** in Tamil Nadu, for caste and gender equality.
- **Maharashtra**: Gopal Baba Walangkar and later **Shahu Maharaj** pushed for reserved seats and caste reform.
- **B.R. Ambedkar**: **Mahad Satyagraha (1927)** for the right of untouchables to use a public water tank.

### Two ways of reform
The reformers took two broad paths.
- **Back to old texts:** the Arya Samaj went back to the Vedas.
- **Reason and modern learning:** the Brahmo Samaj stressed reason and one God for all; the Aligarh movement pushed modern education.

> **Watch:** Prarthana Samaj was in **Bombay**; Brahmo Samaj was in **Calcutta**. Do not swap them.

patterns.name: Organisation ↔ founder ↔ year
patterns.howToSpot: "Who founded the X Samaj?" or a match-the-column of Samajs and founders.
steps: Recall the main chain: Brahmo 1828 (Roy), Prarthana 1867 (Atmaram Pandurang), Arya 1875 (Dayanand), Ramakrishna Mission 1897 (Vivekananda).
Add the others: Satyashodhak 1873 (Phule), Theosophical 1875, MAO College 1875.
Match the pair you are surest of, then cut options.
patterns.why: Each organisation has one founder, so one sure pair removes wrong options fast.

example.q:
The Prarthana Samaj was founded in 1867 by:
(a) Ram Mohan Roy (b) Atmaram Pandurang (c) Dayanand Saraswati (d) Keshab Chandra Sen
steps: Roy = Brahmo; Dayanand = Arya; cut (a) and (c).
Keshab Chandra Sen led the Brahmo Samaj later; cut (d).

patterns.name: Reformer ↔ cause or work

steps: Vidyasagar = widow remarriage + *Borno Porichoy*.
Roy = sati; Dayanand = Back to the Vedas + shuddhi.
Phule = girls' school 1848; Narayana Guru = Ezhava rights; Periyar = Self-Respect.

steps: Widow remarriage + 1856 point to one person.
He sent petitions and raised a fund for remarried widows.

patterns.name: Reform laws: year and details

steps: 1829 sati → 1856 widow remarriage → 1891 age of consent (12) → 1929 Sarda Act.
Sarda Act ages: 18 for boys, 14 for girls.
Match each law with its reformer if names are given.
patterns.why: Only four laws are asked, and their years are far apart.

example.q: The Sarda Act (1929) fixed the minimum marriage age at:
steps: Sarda Act = Child Marriage Restraint Act.
Boys 18, girls 14.

patterns.name: Regional and lower-caste movements
patterns.howToSpot: Sree Narayana Guru, Periyar, SNDP, Singh Sabha, Mahad Satyagraha, Satyashodhak.
steps: Kerala = Narayana Guru: Aruvippuram 1888, SNDP Yogam 1903.
Tamil Nadu = Periyar: Self-Respect Movement 1925.
Maharashtra = Phule (1873), Mahad Satyagraha (Ambedkar, 1927); Punjab = Singh Sabha 1873.
patterns.why: Tying each movement to a state removes most wrong options.

example.q: The Self-Respect Movement (1925) was started by:
steps: 1925 + Tamil Nadu + caste and gender equality.
That is Periyar E.V. Ramasamy.

patterns.name: Same year or odd one out
patterns.howToSpot: "Which two were founded in the same year?" or "Which was NOT founded in 1875?"

Remember the clusters: 1873 (Satyashodhak, Singh Sabha) and 1875 (Arya, Theosophical, MAO).
Pick the pair that shares a year, or the one that breaks it.
patterns.why: Two year clusters cover most of these questions.

example.q:
Which of these was NOT founded in 1875?
(a) Arya Samaj (b) Theosophical Society (c) Ramakrishna Mission (d) MAO College, Aligarh
steps: Arya, Theosophical and MAO are the 1875 trio.
Ramakrishna Mission is 1897.

patterns.howToSpot: "Arrange in chronological order" with three or four reform bodies.
steps: Write the year next to each.
Find the earliest and check which options start with it.
Use the last item to confirm.
patterns.why: Most reform bodies have well-known years, so the order follows directly.

example.q: Arrange in order: 1. Arya Samaj 2. Brahmo Samaj 3. Ramakrishna Mission 4. Prarthana Samaj
steps: Brahmo 1828, Prarthana 1867, Arya 1875, Ramakrishna Mission 1897.

patterns.howToSpot: "Where was X founded?" or "headquarters of" (New York, Adyar, Belur, Bombay, Aligarh).
steps: Theosophical: founded in New York, Indian headquarters at Adyar (Madras).
Ramakrishna Mission: Belur Math. Prarthana and Arya Samaj: Bombay.
Brahmo: Calcutta. Singh Sabha: Amritsar. MAO College: Aligarh.

example.q: The Theosophical Society was first founded at:
steps: It later had its Indian headquarters at Adyar, which is the trap.

Prarthana 1867 (Atmaram Pandurang, Ranade); Satyashodhak 1873 (Phule, Gulamgiri).
1875: Arya Samaj (Dayanand), Theosophical Society (Blavatsky, Olcott), MAO College (Sir Syed).
